primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A due to germline RET gain of function
mechanism: MEN2 is caused by heterozygous germline gain-of-function variants in RET, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase. Constitutive or dysregulated RET signaling promotes C-cell and adrenal medullary tumorigenesis; MEN2A also predisposes to parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma.
vignette: Several members of a family have medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism. Genetic testing identifies a heterozygous pathogenic RET variant.
lead: Which molecular alteration best explains this syndrome?
correct: Constitutive gain-of-function signaling by a receptor tyrosine kinase
distractors: Biallelic loss of a nuclear tumor-suppressor protein that regulates transcription
Loss of a GTPase-activating protein that normally suppresses RAS signaling
Loss of a ubiquitin-ligase component that normally targets HIF for degradation
Loss of mitochondrial succinate dehydrogenase activity with succinate accumulation
distractor_notes: MEN1 involves loss of the nuclear tumor-suppressor menin and produces a different endocrine tumor spectrum.
NF1 loss removes a RAS-GAP and can predispose to pheochromocytoma, but it does not explain the MEN2A triad with a pathogenic RET variant.
VHL loss stabilizes HIF and predisposes to VHL-associated tumors, including pheochromocytoma, but not the classic RET-driven MEN2A constellation.
SDH-complex loss predisposes to hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma syndromes and is not the RET receptor-tyrosine-kinase mechanism.
key_expl: RET is a proto-oncogene encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase. Germline gain-of-function RET variants cause MEN2. MEN2A classically combines medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia/adenoma. The molecular logic is oncogenic activation, not loss of a tumor-suppressor allele.
objective: Recognize MEN2A as a germline RET receptor-tyrosine-kinase gain-of-function syndrome.
